old_manifest_statement:
In the homogeneous lossless plane-wave model, let $\varepsilon=\operatorname{diag}(\varepsilon_\perp,\varepsilon_\perp,\varepsilon_\parallel)$ with $\varepsilon_\perp,\varepsilon_\parallel>0$ in $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$, let $\mu>0$ be a scalar in $\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$, and let $\omega>0$ be in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. For a nonzero source-free mode with real wavevector $k=(k_x,0,k_z)\ne0$ in $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, the nonzero-mode wavevectors lie on exactly the following two sheets:

$$k_x^2+k_z^2=\mu\varepsilon_\perp\omega^2,\qquad \frac{k_x^2}{\varepsilon_\parallel}+\frac{k_z^2}{\varepsilon_\perp}=\mu\omega^2.$$

Away from an intersection the first sheet is the ordinary sector, whose electric amplitude is parallel to $\hat y$, and the second is the extraordinary sector, whose electric amplitude lies in the $xz$ plane; each then has a one-dimensional polarization space. At an intersection the two sectors span a two-dimensional polarization space. If $\varepsilon_\perp=\varepsilon_\parallel$, the sheets coincide in every direction on the common sphere and that complex transverse polarization space is two-dimensional; the ordinary/extraordinary labels then denote the two coordinate sectors, not distinct dispersion branches. If $\varepsilon_\perp\ne\varepsilon_\parallel$, the sheets intersect only for $k_x=0$ and $k_z^2=\mu\varepsilon_\perp\omega^2$; at those optic-axis directions the polarization space is again two-dimensional. The zero amplitude is not a mode in this statement.
new_statement:
In the homogeneous lossless plane-wave model, let $\varepsilon=\operatorname{diag}(\varepsilon_\perp,\varepsilon_\perp,\varepsilon_\parallel)$ with $\varepsilon_\perp,\varepsilon_\parallel>0$ in $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$, let $\mu>0$ be a scalar in $\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$, and let $\omega>0$ be in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. For a nonzero source-free mode with real wavevector $k=(k_x,0,k_z)\ne0$ in $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, the nonzero-mode wavevectors lie on exactly the following two sheets:

$$k_x^2+k_z^2=\mu\varepsilon_\perp\omega^2,\qquad \frac{k_x^2}{\varepsilon_\parallel}+\frac{k_z^2}{\varepsilon_\perp}=\mu\omega^2.$$

Away from an intersection the first sheet is the ordinary sector, whose electric amplitude is parallel to $\hat y$, and the second is the extraordinary sector, whose electric amplitude lies in the $xz$ plane; each then has a one-dimensional polarization space. At an intersection the two sectors span a two-dimensional polarization space. If $\varepsilon_\perp=\varepsilon_\parallel=\varepsilon$, the isotropic specialization also allows arbitrary real $k\ne0$, without the $xz$-plane restriction: its nonzero-mode wavevectors lie in every direction on the common sphere $|k|^2=\mu\varepsilon\omega^2$, and at every such wavevector the polarization space is the two-dimensional complex subspace $\{e\in\mathbb C^3:k\cdot e=0\}$. In the $xz$ section the ordinary/extraordinary labels then denote the two coordinate sectors, not distinct dispersion branches. If $\varepsilon_\perp\ne\varepsilon_\parallel$, the sheets intersect only for $k_x=0$ and $k_z^2=\mu\varepsilon_\perp\omega^2$; at those optic-axis directions the polarization space is again two-dimensional. The zero amplitude is not a mode in this statement.

source_frontmatter_proposal.old: "Conditional classification of nonzero real-wavevector source-free bulk plane-wave modes whose wavevectors are restricted to the xz-plane, in a homogeneous lossless uniaxial dielectric with positive real principal permittivities and positive scalar permeability, in the material-rest frame and SI units. Interfaces, absorption, spatial dispersion and empirical material claims are outside scope."
source_frontmatter_proposal.new: Conditional classification of nonzero real-wavevector source-free bulk plane-wave modes in a homogeneous lossless uniaxial dielectric with positive real principal permittivities and positive scalar permeability, in the material-rest frame and SI units. The general uniaxial classification uses the xz-plane section; the isotropic specialization covers all real-wavevector directions. Interfaces, absorption, spatial dispersion and empirical material claims are outside scope.

old_manifest_statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Choose a one-oscillator Lorentz response with $\varepsilon_\infty>0$ in $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$, $a>0$ in $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, $\omega_0>0$ and $\gamma>0$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and fix $\omega>0$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. In the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention its scalar absolute permittivity is $\varepsilon(\omega)=\varepsilon_\infty+a/(\omega_0^2-\omega^2-i\gamma\omega)$. Let the tensor coefficients be $\boldsymbol\varepsilon(\omega)=\varepsilon(\omega)I_3$ and $\boldsymbol\mu=\mu I_3$ with real $\mu>0$ in $\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$. These coefficients satisfy the transpose-symmetry condition of the reciprocal phasor model, while $\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon(\omega)>0$. For any nonzero local electric amplitude $e\in\mathbb C^3$ in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, the polarization current has amplitude $j=-i\omega(\varepsilon(\omega)-\varepsilon_\infty)e$ in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$. Its cycle-averaged work density on the electric field is

$$\overline q:=\frac1T\int_0^T J_{\mathrm{pol}}(t)\cdot E(t)\,dt=\frac{\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon(\omega)|e|^2>0,\qquad T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega},\qquad |e|^2:=e^*\cdot e=\sum_{r=1}^3|e_r|^2.$$

Here $e^*$ is componentwise complex conjugation. The conjugate used in this cycle average is distinct from the bilinear, unconjugated product in the reciprocity identity.

Thus the coefficient condition that supplies the Lorentz reciprocity identity is compatible with positive absorption in this adopted model.
new_statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Choose a one-oscillator Lorentz response with $\varepsilon_\infty>0$ in $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$, $a>0$ in $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, $\omega_0>0$ and $\gamma>0$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and fix $\omega>0$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. In the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention its scalar absolute permittivity is $\varepsilon(\omega)=\varepsilon_\infty+a/(\omega_0^2-\omega^2-i\gamma\omega)$. Let $I_3$ denote the $3\times3$ identity matrix, and let the tensor coefficients be $\boldsymbol\varepsilon(\omega)=\varepsilon(\omega)I_3$ and $\boldsymbol\mu=\mu I_3$ with real $\mu>0$ in $\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$. These coefficients satisfy the transpose-symmetry condition of the reciprocal phasor model, while $\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon(\omega)>0$. For any nonzero local electric amplitude $e\in\mathbb C^3$ in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, define the real electric field at a fixed material point by $E(t)=\operatorname{Re}(e e^{-i\omega t})$. Let $p_1=(\varepsilon(\omega)-\varepsilon_\infty)e$ be the oscillator polarization amplitude from the one-oscillator response, in $\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}$; put $P_1(t)=\operatorname{Re}(p_1e^{-i\omega t})$, and define its polarization-current contribution by $J_{\mathrm{osc}}(t):=\partial_tP_1(t)$. Its phasor amplitude is $j_{\mathrm{osc}}=-i\omega(\varepsilon(\omega)-\varepsilon_\infty)e$ in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$. The cycle-averaged power density transferred from the electric field to the oscillator through this current contribution, in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$, is

$$\overline q_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac1T\int_0^T J_{\mathrm{osc}}(t)\cdot E(t)\,dt=\frac{\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon(\omega)|e|^2>0,\qquad T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega},\qquad |e|^2:=e^*\cdot e=\sum_{r=1}^3|e_r|^2.$$

Here $e^*$ is componentwise complex conjugation. The conjugate used in this cycle average is distinct from the bilinear, unconjugated product in the reciprocity identity.

Thus the coefficient condition that supplies the Lorentz reciprocity identity is compatible with positive cycle-averaged work on the oscillator-current contribution in this adopted model.
